Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
lowercase messy working request for the film society copy, can you turn this into a usable prompt for writing the right piece, not write the piece itself. we are Lantern Film Society at Northbridge College and we're preparing for a screening of The Glass Orchard, directed by Nia Vale and released in 2018. the date on our calendar is Thursday, October 22, and the screening is at 6:30 p.m. in Bell Hall 204. Doors open at 6:10. The room has 48 seats, admission is free, and people need to reserve a seat by October 20. We have already reserved the room and put the film on our program, but that is not the same thing as having the screening rights, so don't treat those arrangements as permission. At the moment, written permission for a public screening is still pending. The wording needs to make the condition matter, not just mention it somewhere and then carry on as if everything is approved.

The main piece we need is a public event announcement, but it is allowed only if written permission for the public screening has been confirmed by the time the copy is prepared. If it has been confirmed, write the announcement for students and other people in the college community, with the film title, director, year, date, start time, room, doors-open time, free admission, and reservation deadline. Keep it welcoming and straightforward, not grand or like a review. It should make clear what people can do and when they should arrive, and it must not claim anything about the story, quality, awards, or response to the film that isn't in the details here. We don't have a plot summary in these notes, and I don't want one invented to make the announcement sound fuller. Don't add a ticket price, a booking link, or a contact person; none is provided. The announcement should fit a college film society's ordinary event listing and not sound like a commercial cinema advert.

If the written permission has not been confirmed when the copy is prepared, do a different useful thing instead: draft an email to the distributor's screening-rights team asking about permission for this proposed public screening. Don't make the public announcement in that case, not even as a second option, because we can't promote a public screening as cleared while permission is pending. The email should identify the film, director and release year, our society and college, and the planned screening date, time and venue, so the recipient knows what permission we are asking about. Ask whether written permission can be granted for this screening, and ask what screening terms or fee would apply. The request should be polite and practical, not sound like we have already booked a license or expect the answer to be yes. No distributor contact name or email address is in the information, so don't make one up and don't put in a fake address. A subject line is useful for the email, but it should not imply that approval has already been granted.

Some context for the tone: Lantern Film Society usually has students setting up the room, and the listings are read by people who might not know the society yet. We want the event information to feel approachable and easy to scan. The society coordinator described the aim this way: “we want the room to feel welcoming, not like a lecture.” If the permission condition allows the announcement, the line can guide its tone, but don't turn the quote into a new factual claim about the film or a promise about a discussion. The notes don't say there will be a guest, a post-film talk, refreshments, subtitles, or any special access arrangement, so those things are not part of the request. The event is free, but a reservation is still required because there are only 48 seats. Keep those two details together accurately rather than suggesting that people can simply arrive without reserving.

There are a couple of small logistics that matter because we have had people mix them up before. The published screening time is 6:30 p.m., not the doors-open time of 6:10 p.m.; include both with their correct labels if you write the announcement. The reservation deadline is October 20, two days before the screening. Don't change it to the event date, and don't suggest reservations are available after that date. Bell Hall 204 is the room, not a building name or an online venue. We don't have a reservation URL in this request, so refer to the reservation requirement and deadline without inventing a method for making one. The copy should use the supplied details rather than resolve those gaps by guessing.

1. Choose the branch from the permission status at the time of writing. Written permission is currently pending. If the supplied status has changed and permission is confirmed, produce only the public announcement. If it remains unconfirmed, produce only the distributor email. In either branch, don't include both pieces, a note explaining the choice, or a separate checklist. The final response is meant to be directly usable as the selected piece, not an explanation of how it was drafted. Keep the condition tied specifically to written permission for this public screening; having the room, listing, date, or film selection settled does not satisfy it.

For the announcement branch, keep it concise enough to work in the society's event listing while including every event detail above. It can have a brief invitation, but don't add claims about what attendees will experience beyond the supplied logistics and the film screening. For the email branch, keep it focused on the permission question, identify the proposed event clearly, and ask about the applicable terms or fee without assuming either. The email is an inquiry, not a cancellation notice and not a request to announce the event. In both cases, preserve the distinction between a fact we know, such as the scheduled time, and a condition that remains pending, such as permission.

One last detail for the eventual copy: the film's exact title is The Glass Orchard, the director's name is Nia Vale, and the release year is 2018. Use those as given. Please organize these notes into a clear prompt that asks for the conditional choice and sets out the relevant details and limits. The final paragraph should keep the date, time and permission point distinct from the venue and reservation logistics; we need the prompt to be complete, but it should not add a recommendation, approval, or an invented outcome.", "output": "Write one finished piece for Lantern Film Society at Northbridge College, choosing the correct branch according to the status of written permission for a public screening of *The Glass Orchard* at the time you prepare the copy. If permission remains unconfirmed, write only an email to the distributor’s screening-rights team. Do not include both pieces, explain your choice, or add a checklist. **If written permission is confirmed:** Write a welcoming, straightforward announcement for students and others in the college community. Make clear that this is an inquiry, not an assumption that a license has been booked or approval granted. A subject line is useful, but it must not imply approval. The screening date is Thursday, October 22, but the date, time, and permission status are separate from the venue and reservation logistics. Return only the selected, finished piece, with no explanation or invented outcome."}]
